analysis.one_liner: Tightens federal rail safety rules for trains carrying hazardous materials, including detectors, inspections, and much larger fines.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan rail safety bill written after the East Palestine derailment drew 15 cosponsors from both parties but never received a committee vote, dying in a House subcommittee when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill, written in response to the February 2023 derailment in East Palestine, Ohio, would have required the Department of Transportation to write new safety rules for trains carrying hazardous materials: advance notice to state emergency officials, fewer blocked road crossings, limits on train length and weight, and defect-detecting sensors every 10 miles on major railroads. It would also raise maximum federal fines on railroads roughly tenfold, force older tank cars out of flammable-liquid service a year early, and charge each Class I railroad a $1 million annual fee to fund training for local first responders. It never received a committee vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live and work along freight rail lines, especially communities near routes carrying hazardous materials, gain stronger derailment protections: mandated hot-box detectors, more thorough inspections, smaller and slower trains, and an earlier phase-out of older tank cars. Local fire departments and emergency responders gain expanded federal training grants funded by a new fee on the largest railroads. Drivers and pedestrians gain from requirements to reduce blocked rail crossings, and rail mechanical workers gain from rules guaranteeing inspectors adequate time to inspect cars.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Transportation Department to write safety rules for hazmat trains based on the National Transportation Safety Board's East Palestine report, including advance notice and information to state and tribal emergency response officials, a written gas discharge plan, and requirements to reduce or eliminate blocked road crossings, plus rules on train length, weight, speed, route selection, and track and bridge maintenance.

Mandates wayside defect detectors for trains carrying hazardous materials, requiring all Class I railroads to install a hot-box detector every 10 miles of track, with standards for maintenance, alert thresholds, and the actions crews must take when a detector warns of a possible wheel bearing failure — the failure that caused the East Palestine derailment. It also requires safety placards that can withstand heat above 180 degrees.

Requires minimum time a qualified mechanical inspector must spend on each rail car and locomotive carrying hazardous materials, ends abbreviated pre-departure inspections for those cars, and requires audits of federal rail car inspection programs, with each Class I railroad audited at least once every five years.

Raises maximum civil penalties for rail safety violations roughly tenfold — for example from $75,000 to at least $750,000 and from $25,000 to at least $250,000, or a percentage of the railroad's annual income if that is larger — so fines are large enough to matter to multi-billion-dollar carriers.
Phases out older DOT-111 tank cars from flammable-liquid service by May 1, 2028, one year sooner than current law requires, regardless of train makeup.

Creates a new $1 million annual fee on each Class I railroad to fund hazardous-materials training grants for local emergency responders, and doubles the annual supplemental training grant amount from $2 million to $4 million.

analysis.who_pays: The Class I freight railroads — Union Pacific, BNSF, CSX, Norfolk Southern and their peers — bear the direct costs: installing and maintaining detectors every 10 miles, more thorough and more frequent inspections, an earlier tank-car replacement deadline, fines up to ten times larger, and a $1 million annual training fee. Railroads typically pass freight compliance costs to shippers, so some of the cost would ultimately show up in the prices of goods moved by rail.

drawbacks.text: The direct costs — hot-box detectors every 10 miles, guaranteed inspection time, and replacing DOT-111 tank cars a year early — fall on the railroads, which generally pass compliance costs to shippers and, ultimately, to consumer prices for rail-shipped goods.

The core safety rules do not take effect on their own: the bill ties them to regulations issued after the National Transportation Safety Board's East Palestine report, and they apply only to trains not already covered by existing high-hazard flammable train rules, leaving coverage of other hazmat traffic to later rulemaking.

Mandates on train length, weight, and speed were the most contested parts of the post-East Palestine debate; railroads argued such operating limits would raise freight costs without a proportional safety gain, and the bill resolves that fight by flat requirement rather than through a cost-benefit standard.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits and costs are lopsided in opposite directions: the costs land on a handful of highly profitable freight railroads, while the benefits — fewer derailments in towns along the tracks, faster and better-informed emergency response, shorter waits at blocked crossings — are spread across the public and are hard to price but potentially large, as East Palestine showed. The weakest design feature is that the main safety rules wait on a future NTSB report and rulemaking rather than taking direct effect, and the $1 million-per-carrier fee is small relative to the training need. On balance it is a conventional, modestly drafted safety bill whose main cost is money to a concentrated industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in a House Transportation and Infrastructure subcommittee for nearly two years without a markup or a floor vote, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Johnson introduced the bill on March 17, 2023, six weeks after the East Palestine, Ohio derailment, with ten original cosponsors including both Republicans and Democrats from Ohio.
It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and, three days later, to its Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials, where it remained.
Over the next 22 months the subcommittee never held a markup and the House never voted on the bill.

In January 2024, Rep. Emilia Sykes took over as first sponsor — a routine step after the original sponsor's departure from the House — to keep adding cosponsors, and 15 members had signed on by the end, split 8 Democrats and 7 Republicans.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with no further action, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Class I freight railroads are better off: they avoided new detector mandates, tenfold fines, a $1 million annual fee, tighter inspection rules, and an earlier tank-car phase-out, while communities along hazmat rail routes got no new federal protections.

for.name: Rep. Bill Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the RAIL Act in March 2023, weeks after the East Palestine derailment in the district's state, and assembled a bipartisan group of Ohio original cosponsors.

for.name: Rep. Emilia Sykes
for.what_they_did: Took over first sponsorship of the bill by unanimous consent in January 2024 to continue adding cosponsors after the original sponsor's departure.

for.name: Bipartisan Ohio House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed onto the bill, giving it support from both parties concentrated in the state most affected by the derailment.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or reported the bill out; it sat in the Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials subcommittee from March 2023 until the Congress ended.

against.name: Class I freight railroads
against.what_they_did: The industry the bill would fine, fee, and regulate — the major carriers campaigned against post-East Palestine safety mandates such as train-length limits and new detector requirements.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was genuinely bipartisan — a Republican sponsor and 15 cosponsors split 8 Democrats and 7 Republicans, mostly from Ohio — and the bill was never voted on, so no roll-call ever split by party.

industries.note: The bill would have raised maximum safety fines roughly tenfold, imposed a $1 million annual fee, required hot-box detectors every 10 miles on hazmat routes, tightened inspection requirements, and moved up the DOT-111 tank-car phase-out by a year — direct compliance costs for the major carriers. The bill's death leaves these carriers free of all of them, and their interest ran against new mandates the public would have benefited from.
Moving the deadline to retire DOT-111 tank cars up to May 1, 2028 would have forced earlier replacement with DOT-117-specification cars, increasing demand for new, safer tank cars and retrofit work.

industries.industry: Local emergency response and hazmat training providers
industries.note: The bill would have doubled supplemental training grant funding and created a dedicated $1 million-per-carrier annual fee stream for first-responder hazardous-materials training grants.
